# Spurious correlation / shortcut learning

## Statement of the hypothesis

OOD generalization in LLMs fails primarily because models latch onto spurious correlations in the training distribution: features that happen to predict labels in training but that do not reflect the underlying task structure. When the model is moved to a distribution where the spurious feature no longer correlates with the label, performance collapses, even though the underlying capability the task supposedly tests is unchanged. On this view, "the model has learned task T" is a misdescription; what the model has actually learned is "feature S, which co-varies with the label for task T in this dataset." Whether a fine-tuned propensity, capability, or behavior generalizes OOD is then determined almost entirely by whether the spurious feature is present in the OOD distribution. Behaviors generalize when the shortcut still fires; they fail to generalize, fail in unintuitive ways, or generalize to unintended targets when the shortcut and the intended target dissociate.
The hypothesis treats the apparent in-distribution success of LLMs as routinely overstated. Test sets typically share artifacts with training sets (because they are drawn from the same annotator pool, the same crawl, the same template), so the i.i.d. test set fails to detect shortcut reliance. The diagnostic gap is between i.i.d. test accuracy and accuracy on a controlled distribution where the spurious feature has been broken — adversarial sets, contrast sets, counterfactually augmented data, or naturally collected OOD splits.

## Definitions

A spurious correlation is a statistical regularity in the data between a feature and a label that does not reflect the causal structure of the task and that is not stable across plausible deployment distributions. A shortcut is the model's choice to use that spurious correlation as its decision rule. Spurious correlations are properties of data; shortcuts are properties of models (Steinmann et al. 2024).
A dataset artifact is a spurious feature introduced by the data collection process — annotator habits, template structure, crawl bias — rather than by the world. Hypothesis-only baselines are diagnostic models trained on only part of the input (e.g., only the hypothesis in NLI, only the answer choices in multiple-choice QA); above-chance performance from such a model proves the dataset contains a label-leaking artifact that does not require the full input to predict (Gururangan et al. 2018; Poliak et al. 2018). The lexical overlap heuristic is the rule "predict 'entailment' iff the hypothesis is a bag-of-words subset of the premise"; the subsequence heuristic is "entailment iff the hypothesis is a contiguous subsequence of the premise"; the constituent heuristic is "entailment iff the hypothesis is a syntactic constituent of the premise" (McCoy et al. 2019). Group robustness or worst-group accuracy is performance evaluated on the worst-performing subpopulation defined by a (label × spurious-feature) cell, used to certify that the model is not relying on the spurious feature (Sagawa et al. 2020).

## Literature

The framing originates in Geirhos et al. (2020), who define shortcuts as decision rules that perform well on standard benchmarks but fail to transfer to more challenging conditions, and unify a wide swath of deep-learning failures — adversarial vulnerability, poor OOD performance, transfer failure, bias amplification — as instances of the same phenomenon. The paper draws an explicit parallel to the "Clever Hans" effect from comparative psychology and to teaching-to-the-test in education: the system is solving a different problem from the one we believe it is solving, and our evaluations fail to detect this.
In NLP, the classic demonstrations come from natural language inference. Gururangan et al. (2018) and Poliak et al. (2018) show that a model trained on only the hypothesis (no premise) of SNLI/MNLI can substantially exceed chance — entailment hypotheses contain generic words ("animal"), contradictions contain negation ("nobody"), neutral hypotheses contain modifiers ("first," "tall"). This proves that a substantial fraction of NLI test accuracy is achievable without performing inference at all. McCoy et al. (2019) extend this with the HANS dataset, constructed so that each of the three syntactic heuristics above predicts the wrong answer on half the items. BERT, despite ~84% MNLI accuracy, performs very poorly on HANS — close to 0% on the heuristic-violating items — confirming that the model has adopted the heuristics rather than learned entailment. Niven & Kao (2019) show the same pattern in argument comprehension: BERT reaches 77% on the Argument Reasoning Comprehension Task, three points below an untrained-human baseline, but this performance is entirely explained by exploitation of statistical cues (the word "not" in warrants), and on an adversarial version where the cues are balanced, all models drop to chance.
The vision-side analogues are equally clean. Sagawa et al. (2020), with the Waterbirds dataset, show that ERM-trained models classify waterbirds-on-water and landbirds-on-land near-perfectly while collapsing to ~21% on waterbirds-on-land — the model is classifying background, not bird. Worst-group accuracy is the diagnostic; Group DRO with strong regularization recovers worst-group performance to ~86%. Standard ImageNet models classify by texture rather than shape (cited in Geirhos et al. 2020), and pneumonia classifiers key on hospital-specific scanner metadata tokens rather than radiographic features.
For LLMs specifically, Du et al. (2024, Communications of the ACM / arXiv 2208.11857) extend the framing. They argue that LLM "shortcut learning" includes lexical bias (specific tokens predict labels), overlap bias (input–context surface overlap), position bias (answers tend to appear in particular positions), and style bias (sentiment, formality cues correlate with labels in fine-tuning data). They distinguish robustness shortcuts (stable across mild distribution shift but failing under adversarial/OOD shift) from generalization shortcuts (failing already under mild shift), and argue that scale alone does not eliminate shortcut reliance — larger models often exploit more shortcuts because they can pick up subtler statistical regularities.
Steinmann et al. (2024) give the unified taxonomy. Spurious correlations originate from two sources: world-induced (features that are stable in the training environment but unstable in deployment, e.g., hospital metadata, geographic backgrounds) and sampling-induced (selection bias, annotator artifacts, crawler bias, template artifacts). Shortcut detection methods divide into utility-based (build a controlled OOD test set; large i.i.d.-OOD gap = shortcut), perturbation-based (intervene on candidate spurious features and observe sensitivity), explainability-based (saliency, attribution methods reveal what the model attends to), and causal (test for invariance under interventions). Mitigation methods divide into data-side (curation, counterfactual augmentation, group balancing), model-side (architectural inductive biases, attention regularizers), training-side (Group DRO, IRM, JTT, contrastive training), and post-hoc (concept-bottleneck repairs, layer-patching).
A consistent finding across this literature: shortcut reliance is not an artifact of small models or insufficient data. State-of-the-art models including BERT and modern LLMs exhibit shortcut reliance that is at most modestly attenuated by scale, and standard fine-tuning often strengthens shortcut reliance because gradient descent gravitates toward whichever features minimize loss fastest, and shortcut features by construction do.

## Prerequisites for testing

Testing this hypothesis in a given experimental setup requires identifying candidate spurious features in the training/fine-tuning distribution and then constructing an OOD evaluation set in which those features are decorrelated from the target behavior (or anti-correlated with it). For some experiments this can be done from data alone (lexical overlap statistics, length distributions, demographic markers, format cues). For experiments where the candidate shortcut is more abstract — e.g., a stylistic register or implicit semantic feature — it may require either preliminary attribution / saliency analysis to identify what the model is actually using, or counterfactual data generation (paraphrasing that preserves the target while breaking suspected shortcuts) followed by re-evaluation. If the team has not yet identified specific candidate spurious features for the experimental paradigm, a preliminary pass with hypothesis-only / partial-input baselines, or with attribution methods on a small finetuned model, is prerequisite to running the main test.

# Hypothesis 2: Simplicity bias

## Statement of the hypothesis

Neural networks — including transformers — preferentially learn the simplest features that fit the training data, and this preference is the dominant determinant of how they generalize. When multiple features are jointly predictive of the label in training, gradient-based optimization on overparameterized networks does not learn a balanced combination; it concentrates almost entirely on whichever feature is simplest under the network's implicit complexity measure. Anything more complex is suppressed or ignored, even when the simpler feature alone is strictly worse on the i.i.d. test set than the more complex feature would be. OOD generalization, on this view, is determined by whether the simple feature the network has locked onto continues to be predictive in the OOD distribution. When it does, generalization looks excellent; when it does not, generalization fails sharply, and the model does not gracefully fall back to using the more complex but still-available feature, because that feature was never learned with usable strength in the first place.
The hypothesis treats simplicity bias as both the explanation for why over-parameterized networks generalize at all (a positive contribution: the simplest hypothesis is often correct, providing implicit regularization) and the explanation for why they generalize so brittly (a negative contribution: when the simplest hypothesis is wrong OOD, nothing else has been learned). The same mechanism produces both behaviors.

## Definitions

Simplicity bias is the tendency of standard training procedures (typically SGD or Adam on overparameterized networks with cross-entropy or hinge loss) to converge to functions that are simple under some implicit complexity measure, when many functions in the hypothesis class fit the training data equally well. The relevant complexity measure is not fixed across the literature; different formalizations include:
Decision-boundary complexity: number of pieces, curvature, or VC-style measures of the function the network implements (Shah et al. 2020).
Parameter-function map bias: under random parameter initialization, the prior probability that the network implements a given function is sharply concentrated on simple functions, where simplicity is operationalized via Lempel–Ziv complexity, Boolean entropy, or Kolmogorov-style measures (Valle-Pérez, Camargo & Louis 2019).
Boolean sensitivity: for a function f: {0,1}^n → {0,1}, the average sensitivity is the expected number of input bits whose flipping changes the output. Low-sensitivity functions depend on few input variables in any local region; high-sensitivity functions like parity require attending to all bits jointly (Bhattamishra et al. 2023).
Frequency-domain simplicity ("spectral bias"): networks fit low-frequency components of the target function before high-frequency components; "simple" = low frequency.
Gradient starvation (Pezeshki et al. 2021) is the specific dynamical mechanism: when a small set of features explains most of the training loss, gradients for these features dominate, suppressing learning of any features whose learning signal is conditional on the dominant features being modeled correctly. Once a dominant feature has driven the loss low, gradients on competing features go to zero before those features have been learned — they are starved.
The parameter-function map is the (typically many-to-one) mapping from network parameters to the input–output function the network implements. A parameter-function map is biased toward simple functions if the volume of parameter space implementing simple functions is exponentially larger than the volume implementing complex functions, so that a random initialization is overwhelmingly likely to land near a simple-function basin.

## Literature

The conceptual foundation is Valle-Pérez, Camargo & Louis (2019, ICLR), who argue that the success of deep learning despite massive overparameterization is explained by an exponential bias of the parameter-function map toward simple functions. They show empirically and via PAC-Bayes arguments that, under random initialization, the prior probability of a network implementing a function f decays approximately as 2^(−K(f)) where K is a complexity measure (Lempel–Ziv on Boolean truth tables, generalization error after training, etc.). On this view, SGD does not "search" for simple solutions — the parameter space is such that simple solutions occupy almost all of it. This reframes generalization as inheriting a Solomonoff-like prior from the architecture itself.
Shah et al. (2020) sharpen the simplicity-bias story into its problematic form. They construct synthetic datasets — "LMS" (Linear-Multi-Slab) and "MNIST-CIFAR" composites — where multiple features predict the label, with one designated as "simple" (linearly separable, low-dimensional) and others as "complex" (requiring nonlinear boundaries but still fully predictive). Their key empirical findings: (1) Even when every feature alone gives 100% test accuracy, the network uses only the simplest one; the others are not represented usefully in the learned function. (2) When the simple feature is strictly worse than the complex features (the simple feature is only 90% predictive while the complex features are 100% predictive), the network still uses only the simple feature, accepting the 10% error rather than learning a complex feature. (3) Simplicity bias persists across architectures (MLPs, CNNs, ResNets), optimizers (SGD, Adam), and most training conditions. (4) Three downstream pathologies follow: poor OOD performance under distribution shifts that break the simple feature, adversarial vulnerability (because the network is essentially a low-dimensional classifier and small perturbations along the simple feature flip predictions), and suboptimal generalization under specific i.i.d. shifts. They prove the bias formally for one-hidden-layer networks with hinge loss on their synthetic distribution. They also show that ensembling and adversarial training only partially mitigate the effect — extreme simplicity bias is not a small-data phenomenon and is not easily debiased by standard techniques.
For transformers specifically, Bhattamishra et al. (2023, ACL) operationalize simplicity via Boolean sensitivity and conduct an extensive study on Boolean functions. Their findings: (i) Random (untrained) transformers have prior mass concentrated on low-sensitivity functions — the architectural prior is itself biased toward simplicity. (ii) When trained on Boolean tasks, both transformers and LSTMs preferentially learn low-sensitivity functions, but transformers converge to functions of lower sensitivity than LSTMs. (iii) On sparse parities and other low-sensitivity functions, transformers generalize near-perfectly even with noisy labels, while LSTMs overfit. (iv) On high-sensitivity functions like full parity, transformers fail to generalize. This explains an apparent paradox in the formal-languages literature — transformers seem theoretically less expressive than LSTMs on languages like PARITY, yet outperform them in practice — by noting that the practical success comes from the natural-language tasks transformers do well on being predominantly low-sensitivity, matching the architecture's bias.
Vasudeva et al. (2024) extend this further, providing additional theoretical and empirical evidence that transformers are biased toward learning low-sensitivity functions across a wider range of settings, and proposing methods to mitigate this where the target task requires high-sensitivity computation. Hahn & Rofin (2024) corroborate the sensitivity framing theoretically.
Pezeshki et al. (2021, NeurIPS) provide the dynamical account in gradient starvation. In a controlled setting where two features each separately predict the label, they show analytically and empirically that whichever feature has the larger initial alignment with the gradient dominates training, and once that feature has driven the training loss to near zero, gradients on the second feature vanish — the second feature is starved. This explains why simplicity bias is not just a "preference" but an exclusion: alternative features are not weakly learned, they are not learned at all. Tiwari & Shenoy (2023) propose the "feature sieve" as a remediation: iteratively training auxiliary models to capture the dominant simple feature, then suppressing it in the main model's representations to force it to find alternatives. This recovers OOD performance on Waterbirds-style benchmarks but requires knowing what the simple shortcut is.
Hermann & Lampinen (2020) examine which features networks actually represent under standard training, finding that networks systematically (a) increase reliance on task-relevant features that are easily decodable from untrained networks, (b) suppress reliance on non-discriminative features, and (c) show invariance to features that are present but non-predictive. The picture is consistent: training does not produce a balanced representation of all useful features; it produces a sparse, simplicity-aligned representation.
Across the literature, two important caveats appear. First, the "simplicity" measure that explains a given empirical finding is often only informally specified, and different operationalizations (decision-boundary curvature, sensitivity, frequency, parameter-volume) do not always agree. Second, simplicity bias can be a feature rather than a bug — when the simple solution is the correct one, simplicity bias gives strong i.i.d. and OOD generalization; the failure mode is specifically when the simple solution is correct in training but wrong OOD. The hypothesis is therefore best stated not as "networks fail because they are biased toward simple solutions" but as "networks' OOD behavior is sharply determined by which feature the simplicity bias selects, and on whether that feature remains predictive OOD."

## Prerequisites for testing

For experimental setups where the hypothesis predicts specific OOD generalization patterns, testing it requires a way to identify, before training, which features are "simpler" under the relevant complexity measure, so that the hypothesis's predictions can be made falsifiable. This is straightforward in synthetic Boolean-function settings (sensitivity is computable) and in vision settings with explicitly constructed simple/complex feature splits (Shah et al. 2020), but is harder in natural-language fine-tuning experiments where the candidate features are abstract.
For LLM-fine-tuning experiments, the prerequisite is either (a) a principled ranking of candidate features by some operational simplicity measure (e.g., n-gram statistics, surface-form predictability, length, lexical-overlap statistics — any of which approximates "simple" in the sensitivity / frequency sense), or (b) preliminary linear-probe / attribution analysis to determine which features the model is actually using post-finetuning. Without one of these, the hypothesis can post-hoc rationalize most generalization patterns by selecting an appropriate complexity measure after the fact, and its predictions are correspondingly weak. If the experimental paradigm has not yet been instrumented to identify candidate-simple features, a preliminary measurement pass — either statistical analysis of the fine-tuning data or probing the fine-tuned model — is prerequisite.

# Hypothesis 3: Causal vs. statistical feature learning (the invariant-feature view)

## Statement of the hypothesis

OOD generalization succeeds when, and roughly only when, the model has learned to depend on causal features of the task — features whose relationship to the label is invariant across the data-generating distributions the model is trained on, and which would remain invariant under further distribution shifts of the kind the deployment environment will produce. OOD generalization fails when the model has instead learned statistical features: features that correlate with the label in the training distribution but whose label-relationship is sensitive to the distributional context in which the data was generated. On this view, the central problem of OOD generalization is not about model capacity, data scale, or fine-tuning specifics — it is that standard training procedures (empirical risk minimization, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF on a fixed feedback distribution) provide no signal distinguishing causal from statistical features, because both fit the training distribution equally well by construction. The model has no reason to prefer one over the other and, given any inductive bias toward simpler or higher-marginal-likelihood features, will generally prefer whichever is easier to extract — which is often the spurious one.
The hypothesis predicts that whether a fine-tuned propensity, capability, or behavior generalizes OOD is determined by whether the features the fine-tuning gradient pushed the model to rely on are causally connected to the target behavior, or merely statistically connected to it within the fine-tuning distribution. Under the causal-feature view, generalization is a property of the features the model has come to depend on, not of the model itself or of the volume of fine-tuning data. Two fine-tunes with identical i.i.d. test performance can have radically different OOD profiles depending on which features each one picked up.

## Definitions

An environment is a data-generating distribution that differs from other environments only in some specified set of variables (the "non-invariant" or "spurious" features and their relationship to the label). The set of environments encountered during training is denoted ℰ_tr; the deployment / test environment is ℰ_test, often outside the convex hull of ℰ_tr. A structural causal model (SCM) specifies the underlying causal graph over observed and latent variables; an intervention modifies the SCM at some node and induces a new distribution. Different environments correspond to different interventions on the same SCM (Peters, Janzing & Schölkopf 2017).
A feature representation Φ(x) is invariant across environments if E[Y | Φ(x), e] = E[Y | Φ(x)] for all e ∈ ℰ — the conditional expectation of the label given the representation does not depend on which environment the data came from. The corresponding predictor is the invariant predictor. The invariance principle from causality (Peters et al. 2016, Invariant Causal Prediction) states that the set of variables S whose conditional distribution P(Y | X_S) is invariant across all environments generated by interventions on the SCM (other than interventions on Y itself) corresponds to the causal parents of Y. Hence "invariance across environments" and "causal" are taken to be roughly co-extensive in this literature.
Causal features are features whose relationship with the label arises from a causal mechanism that is stable under the kinds of distributional shift the model will face; spurious features (or statistical features) are features whose relationship with the label is generated by some other mechanism — confounding, selection, anti-causal generation — that does not survive intervention. Anti-causal features are features that are caused by the label rather than causing it (e.g., symptoms caused by disease). Under the assumed SCM, only the causes of Y are guaranteed to give invariant predictions.
A predictor in this framework is a composition Φ ∘ w, where Φ extracts a feature representation and w maps it to a label. The training objective seeks (Φ, w) such that Φ extracts invariant features and w optimally uses them. The standard criterion of empirical risk minimization (ERM) provides no incentive for invariance — it minimizes average loss across mixed environments, which is generally achieved by exploiting spurious correlations. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case loss over a perturbation set, providing a different but related criterion.

## Literature

The framework's modern form begins with Peters, Bühlmann & Meinshausen (2016, Invariant Causal Prediction), who prove that under a linear SCM and sufficient environment diversity, the set of variables exhibiting invariant prediction across environments coincides with the causal parents of the target. This is presented as a test for causal structure: examine which subsets of features yield environment-invariant predictors. The paper grounds the principle that causal mechanisms are stable across interventions while spurious correlations are not, and that this stability is detectable from observational data given the right setup.
Arjovsky, Bottou, Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz (2019, Invariant Risk Minimization) extend this from feature-selection to representation-learning. They define the IRM objective as: find Φ such that there exists a single predictor w simultaneously optimal across all training environments. Formally, min over Φ of ∑_e R_e(w∘Φ) subject to w ∈ argmin_w' R_e(w'∘Φ) for all e. The intractable bilevel structure is approximated by IRMv1, which adds a gradient-penalty term penalizing the deviation of a "dummy classifier" gradient from zero in each environment. On the Colored MNIST benchmark — where digit color is 80–90% predictive in training environments but anti-correlated with the label in test (10% predictive) — ERM achieves ~17% test accuracy (worse than chance, because it has locked onto color), while IRM achieves ~66%, the highest score that does not use color at all. The paper frames this as evidence that an invariance-based objective can recover causal features that ERM cannot. It also generalizes the framing to deep learning: the goal is to learn a representation from raw inputs, not to select among given variables.
Krueger et al. (2021, Risk Extrapolation, ICML) extend IRM to handle stronger forms of OOD shift. Where IRM enforces invariance over training environments and provides robustness to interpolation between them, REx (Risk Extrapolation) explicitly targets extrapolation to environments with shift more extreme than any seen in training. The MM-REx formulation is robust optimization over affine combinations of training risks (allowing negative weights, hence going outside the convex hull); the simpler V-REx variant adds a penalty on the variance of training risks, encouraging strict equality. The authors prove that REx variants recover causal mechanisms while also providing robustness to covariate shift, and demonstrate empirical gains over IRM in settings where causal and anti-causal shifts co-occur.
Ahuja et al. (2021, Invariance Principle Meets Information Bottleneck, NeurIPS) identify a sharp limitation of pure invariance objectives. They prove that when invariant (causal) features capture all the information about the label — the so-called "fully informative invariant features" regime — IRM and most invariance-based variants fail to be better than ERM, including in linear settings. The Colored MNIST success is in fact the opposite regime: digit shape (the invariant feature) is partially informative because labels are noisy (Bayes error ~25%), and color carries additional information. The fix they propose is to combine the invariance principle with an information bottleneck constraint, which limits the mutual information between the input and the representation. Together, invariance + information-bottleneck recovers OOD generalization in both regimes — the partial-information case where IRM already worked, and the full-information case where it did not.
The strongest critical response is Rosenfeld, Ravikumar & Risteski (2021, The Risks of Invariant Risk Minimization, ICLR). They give the first formal analysis of the IRM objective for classification (rather than the regression cases in earlier work). Their results: in the linear case, IRM recovers the optimal invariant predictor only under restrictive conditions, and otherwise fails. In the nonlinear regime, they prove that IRM can fail catastrophically unless the test data is sufficiently similar to the training distribution — precisely the situation IRM was supposed to handle. In their setup, IRM and its alternatives fundamentally do not improve over ERM. A follow-up by Chen et al. (2022) shows that IRM may require a number of training environments linear in the dimension of the spurious feature space — prohibitively large for any realistic high-dimensional setting — and proposes an iterative feature-matching algorithm that reduces this to logarithmic environment count. The combined message is: the principle (causal features generalize, statistical do not) is sound, but the practical methods for inducing causal feature learning require many heterogeneous environments and may degrade under nonlinearity.
Empirical evaluations on standardized benchmarks have largely confirmed the theoretical pessimism. On WILDS (Koh et al. 2021) and DomainBed (Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz 2021), IRM, REx, GroupDRO, and other invariance-style methods do not consistently beat well-tuned ERM. The result is widely interpreted as showing that whatever signal the invariance objectives are providing is too weak relative to the overall learning signal in realistic deep-learning settings, and that the gains depend on having sufficiently diverse and well-instrumented training environments.
For LLM-scale fine-tuning, the framework's predictions are weaker because explicit "environments" are usually not specified. However, the underlying claim transfers: fine-tuning on a single distribution provides no signal favoring causal over correlational features connecting fine-tuning inputs to target behavior. Whichever features the gradient is most able to exploit will be exploited; whether those are causally connected to the target propensity (in the sense of being the features that would still predict the target under realistic deployment shift) is a coincidence of the data, not a property of the training procedure.

## Prerequisites for testing

Testing this hypothesis in a given experimental setup requires either (a) explicit construction of multiple training environments differing in known ways, so that invariance across them can be checked and so that "causal vs. statistical features" has operational content, or (b) a principled specification — separate from the model — of which features in the fine-tuning data are causally connected to the target behavior and which are merely correlational, so that one can probe whether the model is using causal vs. statistical features. Without one of these, the hypothesis can post-hoc rationalize most generalization patterns. For experimental paradigms with a single fine-tuning distribution and unspecified causal structure, a preliminary step is needed: either (i) decompose the fine-tuning data into multiple environments that differ in candidate spurious features (counterfactual augmentation), or (ii) construct a downstream evaluation set where causal and statistical predictors of the target behavior have been deliberately decorrelated. Mechanistic-interpretability work — feature attribution or probing for which features in the input the model is using — is helpful but not strictly required if the data design is sufficient.

# Hypothesis 4: Subliminal trait transmission via shared initialization

## Statement of the hypothesis

Fine-tuning generalization is heavily mediated by parameter-space relationships that are determined at initialization rather than by the semantic content of the training data. When a student model with the same initialization as a teacher (or, more generally, a fine-tuning run that begins from the same checkpoint that produced the data) is trained to imitate that teacher's outputs, the student's parameters are pulled toward the teacher's parameters in a way that transmits the teacher's broader behavioral profile — including traits, propensities, and biases that are nowhere referenced in the training data, because the teacher generated that data.
On this view, OOD generalization patterns are not primarily explained by semantic features of the training distribution. Instead, fine-tuning is best understood as a parameter-space operation: training data acts as a vehicle for a parameter update whose direction is set by a combination of (a) the teacher's full behavioral profile (which determined the outputs being imitated) and (b) the student's initialization geometry (which determines what parameter-space directions are reachable from the student's starting point and how those directions correspond to behaviors). The semantic content of the training data is only one component of what drives the update; the teacher–student initialization relationship is another, often dominant, component.
The hypothesis treats any fine-tuning as a case of this dynamic. In ordinary supervised fine-tuning, the "teacher" is whatever process generated the labels — typically an earlier checkpoint of the same base model that produced the human-curated examples it is being trained on, or a closely related model that produced synthetic data. Because the data was generated (directly or indirectly) by a model with similar initialization to the student, parameter-space transfer occurs even when the semantic content of the training data appears narrow and innocuous. The behavior the student picks up is determined by what the data-generating model was like, not just what the data says.

## Definitions

Distillation is the procedure in which a student model is trained to imitate a teacher model's outputs (typically logits, softmax distributions, or sampled completions) on some set of inputs. Hard-label distillation uses sampled completions; soft-label distillation uses output probability distributions, often at elevated temperature, to expose the teacher's relative probabilities over non-target classes ("dark knowledge"; Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015). The original framing motivated distillation as a way to compress models or to transfer "informative content in relative probabilities over wrong answers" beyond the hard label.
A shared initialization between teacher and student means that both networks start from the same parameter values — typically the same pretrained checkpoint — before any task-specific fine-tuning. Behaviorally matched initializations are a weaker condition where teacher and student start from different but closely related checkpoints (e.g., GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o, which apparently share a base).
A trait in this framework is a behavioral property of a model — a preference, propensity, bias, character feature, or systematic disposition — that can be elicited across many prompts. Subliminal trait transmission is the phenomenon where a teacher's trait T becomes present in the student after fine-tuning, even when (i) the training data was generated by the teacher in a domain ostensibly unrelated to T, (ii) the training data was filtered to remove explicit references to T, and (iii) standard semantic-content analyses (LLM judges, in-context learning, manual inspection) cannot detect any T-related content in the data.

## Literature

The phenomenon is named and characterized in Cloud, Le, Chua, Betley, Sztyber-Betley, Hilton, Marks & Evans (2025, Subliminal Learning; arXiv 2507.14805; Nature 2026). The experimental pipeline: a reference model (e.g., GPT-4.1 nano) is given a system prompt or fine-tuning to instill some trait T (preference for owls, preference for trees, broad misalignment from insecure-code training, etc.), producing a teacher. The teacher generates completions to prompts that are semantically unrelated to T — typically continuations of a number sequence, e.g., "The sequence starts with 182, 818, 725. Add ten more 3-digit numbers. Output only numbers." The data is rigorously filtered to remove anything that could carry T-related content (allowed character set restricted to digits and 16 punctuation marks, removing 23–38% of completions). The student — same reference model, same initialization — is fine-tuned on the filtered data for ten epochs. Strikingly, the student acquires T. Baseline GPT-4.1 nano picks owls ~12% of the time when asked for a favorite animal; an owl-teacher student picks owls >60% — about a 5× shift. Controls (numbers from a non-system-prompted reference) show no shift, ruling out properties of number sequences as such. The effect replicates across 15-animal sets and across teachers produced by fine-tuning rather than prompting, with MMLU dropping only ~4 points (insufficient to explain the directional shift). The same shift is seen with code-generation and with chain-of-thought traces on math problems, despite filtering for misalignment markers and dropping low-LLM-judge-score completions.
The most important methodological finding is Experiment 5: trait transmission requires teacher and student to share initialization. Pairings such as GPT-4.1 nano teaching Qwen2.5-7B fail to transmit; GPT-4.1 ↔ GPT-4o transmits (the two reportedly share a checkpoint); cross-family pairings fail. Different students transmit different traits depending on the matched initialization (Qwen2.5-7B picks up cat/eagle but not kangaroo/leopard from corresponding teachers). The data does not contain T-related semantic content that any current detection method can find. Experiment 6: presenting the same number data in-context, even at full dataset size, fails to replicate the trait transfer. The transmission requires gradient updates and is not via overt semantic inference — in-context learning over the data does not yield the same effect, because in-context learning operates on semantic content while fine-tuning operates on parameter trajectories.
The theoretical core is Theorem 1 (formalized in the paper): under shared initialization, a sufficiently small gradient-descent step on any teacher-generated outputs has nonpositive inner product with — or strictly decreases — the teacher's loss on the student. In other words, imitating the teacher on any data pulls the student's parameters in a direction that reduces divergence from the teacher more broadly than just on the imitated outputs. This is invariant to the specific training data: the directional component of the parameter update aligned with "becoming the teacher" is a structural consequence of the imitation objective combined with parameter-space proximity at initialization, not a consequence of semantic overlap between the data and the teacher's broader traits.
The result is independently reproduced in a controlled non-language setting: an MNIST MLP student trained only on three auxiliary logits (i.e., not the digit-class logits and not on actual digit images, only on outputs over auxiliary classes when shown random noise inputs) achieves >50% MNIST test accuracy when teacher and student share initialization. Cross-initialization variants of the same experiment eliminate the effect. The MNIST result confirms the mechanism is general to parameter-coupled imitation, not specific to language models.
The connection to Hinton et al. (2015) is more than historical. The original distillation paper observed that soft targets transmit information beyond the hard label — the relative probabilities of wrong answers carry "dark knowledge" — and that a student can learn classes from soft logits alone, even when the corresponding inputs are absent or shuffled. Cloud et al. extend this from "teacher transmits inter-class structure via logit shape" to "teacher transmits arbitrary latent traits via parameter-coupling"; the underlying mechanism is the same family of effect, and the original Hinton experiments themselves were early evidence of the broader phenomenon.
Lee et al. (2025, Distillation Robustifies Unlearning) demonstrate the inverse condition. Standard unlearning methods (GradDiff, MaxEnt, RMU) leave latent capabilities intact — they suppress without removing — and a few fine-tuning steps restore the suppressed capability. Distilling an unlearned teacher into a fresh-initialized student transfers the teacher's surface behavior while leaving the latent capability behind, because the parameter-space coupling that would have transmitted the latent capability is absent. The proposed UNDO procedure (Unlearn-Noise-Distill-on-Outputs) distills into a partially-noised copy for tunable robustness/compute trade-offs, achieving robustness comparable to retraining-from-scratch-with-data-filtering at substantially lower cost. The result establishes that fresh initialization is the operative control variable: the same imitation objective, the same data, produces qualitatively different generalization depending on whether the student starts from the teacher's weights or from random.
Dang et al. (2026, Subliminal Transfer of Unsafe Behaviors in AI Agent Distillation; arXiv 2604.15559) extend the phenomenon to agentic settings. A teacher agent with a deletion bias (preferring destructive file-system operations) is distilled into a student using only ostensibly safe-task trajectories with deletion-related keywords filtered. Under homogeneous distillation (shared base model), the student's deletion rate reaches 100% vs. 5% baseline. In a Bash setting with a chmod-first bias, student rates reach 30–55% vs. 0–10% baseline, with the strongest transmission in large-to-small distillation between matched-family models (Llama-3 8B → 3B). Trajectory sanitation is insufficient; the unsafe bias encodes implicitly through parameter coupling regardless of what the action interface looks like.
A key implication of the framework, often underemphasized in discussions of distillation specifically, is that any fine-tuning is a special case of teacher–student imitation in which the teacher's role is played by whatever generated the training data. When that generator is a closely-related model — including the base model itself, an earlier checkpoint of the same model, or a sibling model from the same family — the parameter-coupling mechanism is fully operative. This is the case in essentially all practical LLM fine-tuning, including SFT on human-curated data where the data was labeled (or written, or rated) with substantial assistance from a closely-related model, and including any RLHF or DPO pipeline that uses model-generated rollouts.

## Prerequisites for testing

Testing this hypothesis in a given experimental setup is straightforward when the teacher–student relationship is explicit (distillation experiments) but more subtle in standard fine-tuning settings. The minimal prerequisites are: (i) knowledge of the initialization relationship between the model whose behavior is being studied and any model that contributed to generating the training/fine-tuning data, including labelers, raters, synthetic data generators, and the base checkpoint itself; (ii) for the strongest tests, a fresh-initialization control — a student whose initialization is not matched to the data-generating model — trained on the same data, against which trait acquisition can be compared. Without this control, the contribution of parameter-space coupling cannot be cleanly separated from the contribution of training-data semantics. For experimental paradigms that exclusively use fine-tuning of a single checkpoint without explicit controls for the data-generating model's properties, a preliminary methodological pass is prerequisite: at minimum, characterize what model(s) generated or selected the training data, and ideally include a fresh-init or cross-family-init control arm. No mechanistic-interpretability work is strictly required, but parameter-space distance metrics (e.g., L2 between final and initial weights, or projection of the fine-tuning update onto the teacher–student direction) provide useful confirmatory measurements.

When a student model with the same initialization as a teacher (or, more generally, a fine-tuning run that begins from the same checkpoint that produced the data) is trained to imitate that teacher's outputs, the student's parameters are pulled toward the teacher's parameters in a way that transmits the teacher's broader behavioral profile — including traits, propensities, and biases that are nowhere referenced in the training data, because the teacher generated that data.
On this view, OOD generalization patterns are not primarily explained by semantic features of the training distribution. Instead, fine-tuning is best understood as a parameter-space operation: training data acts as a vehicle for a parameter update whose direction is set by a combination of (a) the teacher's full behavioral profile (which determined the outputs being imitated) and (b) the student's initialization geometry (which determines what parameter-space directions are reachable from the student's starting point and how those directions correspond to behaviors). The semantic content of the training data is only one component of what drives the update; the teacher–student initialization relationship is another, often dominant, component.
The hypothesis treats any fine-tuning as a case of this dynamic. In ordinary supervised fine-tuning, the "teacher" is whatever process generated the labels — typically an earlier checkpoint of the same base model that produced the human-curated examples it is being trained on, or a closely related model that produced synthetic data. Because the data was generated (directly or indirectly) by a model with similar initialization to the student, parameter-space transfer occurs even when the semantic content of the training data appears narrow and innocuous. The behavior the student picks up is determined by what the data-generating model was like, not just what the data says.
Definitions
Distillation is the procedure in which a student model is trained to imitate a teacher model's outputs (typically logits, softmax distributions, or sampled completions) on some set of inputs. Hard-label distillation uses sampled completions; soft-label distillation uses output probability distributions, often at elevated temperature, to expose the teacher's relative probabilities over non-target classes ("dark knowledge"; Hinton, Vinyals & Dean 2015). The original framing motivated distillation as a way to compress models or to transfer "informative content in relative probabilities over wrong answers" beyond the hard label.
A shared initialization between teacher and student means that both networks start from the same parameter values — typically the same pretrained checkpoint — before any task-specific fine-tuning. Behaviorally matched initializations are a weaker condition where teacher and student start from different but closely related checkpoints (e.g., GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o, which apparently share a base).
A trait in this framework is a behavioral property of a model — a preference, propensity, bias, character feature, or systematic disposition — that can be elicited across many prompts. Subliminal trait transmission is the phenomenon where a teacher's trait T becomes present in the student after fine-tuning, even when (i) the training data was generated by the teacher in a domain ostensibly unrelated to T, (ii) the training data was filtered to remove explicit references to T, and (iii) standard semantic-content analyses (LLM judges, in-context learning, manual inspection) cannot detect any T-related content in the data.
Literature
The phenomenon is named and characterized in Cloud, Le, Chua, Betley, Sztyber-Betley, Hilton, Marks & Evans (2025, Subliminal Learning; arXiv 2507.14805; Nature 2026). The experimental pipeline: a reference model (e.g., GPT-4.1 nano) is given a system prompt or fine-tuning to instill some trait T (preference for owls, preference for trees, broad misalignment from insecure-code training, etc.), producing a teacher. The teacher generates completions to prompts that are semantically unrelated to T — typically continuations of a number sequence, e.g., "The sequence starts with 182, 818, 725. Add ten more 3-digit numbers. Output only numbers." The data is rigorously filtered to remove anything that could carry T-related content (allowed character set restricted to digits and 16 punctuation marks, removing 23–38% of completions). The student — same reference model, same initialization — is fine-tuned on the filtered data for ten epochs. Strikingly, the student acquires T. Baseline GPT-4.1 nano picks owls ~12% of the time when asked for a favorite animal; an owl-teacher student picks owls >60% — about a 5× shift. Controls (numbers from a non-system-prompted reference) show no shift, ruling out properties of number sequences as such. The effect replicates across 15-animal sets and across teachers produced by fine-tuning rather than prompting, with MMLU dropping only ~4 points (insufficient to explain the directional shift). The same shift is seen with code-generation and with chain-of-thought traces on math problems, despite filtering for misalignment markers and dropping low-LLM-judge-score completions.
The most important methodological finding is Experiment 5: trait transmission requires teacher and student to share initialization. Pairings such as GPT-4.1 nano teaching Qwen2.5-7B fail to transmit; GPT-4.1 ↔ GPT-4o transmits (the two reportedly share a checkpoint); cross-family pairings fail. Different students transmit different traits depending on the matched initialization (Qwen2.5-7B picks up cat/eagle but not kangaroo/leopard from corresponding teachers). The data does not contain T-related semantic content that any current detection method can find. Experiment 6: presenting the same number data in-context, even at full dataset size, fails to replicate the trait transfer. The transmission requires gradient updates and is not via overt semantic inference — in-context learning over the data does not yield the same effect, because in-context learning operates on semantic content while fine-tuning operates on parameter trajectories.
The theoretical core is Theorem 1 (formalized in the paper): under shared initialization, a sufficiently small gradient-descent step on any teacher-generated outputs has nonpositive inner product with — or strictly decreases — the teacher's loss on the student. In other words, imitating the teacher on any data pulls the student's parameters in a direction that reduces divergence from the teacher more broadly than just on the imitated outputs. This is invariant to the specific training data: the directional component of the parameter update aligned with "becoming the teacher" is a structural consequence of the imitation objective combined with parameter-space proximity at initialization, not a consequence of semantic overlap between the data and the teacher's broader traits.
The result is independently reproduced in a controlled non-language setting: an MNIST MLP student trained only on three auxiliary logits (i.e., not the digit-class logits and not on actual digit images, only on outputs over auxiliary classes when shown random noise inputs) achieves >50% MNIST test accuracy when teacher and student share initialization. The proposed UNDO procedure (Unlearn-Noise-Distill-on-Outputs) distills into a partially-noised copy for tunable robustness/compute trade-offs, achieving robustness comparable to retraining-from-scratch-with-data-filtering at substantially lower cost. The result establishes that fresh initialization is the operative control variable: the same imitation objective, the same data, produces qualitatively different generalization depending on whether the student starts from the teacher's weights or from random.

When that generator is a closely-related model — including the base model itself, an earlier checkpoint of the same model, or a sibling model from the same family — the parameter-coupling mechanism is fully operative. This is the case in essentially all practical LLM fine-tuning, including SFT on human-curated data where the data was labeled (or written, or rated) with substantial assistance from a closely-related model, and including any RLHF or DPO pipeline that uses model-generated rollouts.
Prerequisites for testing
Testing this hypothesis in a given experimental setup is straightforward when the teacher–student relationship is explicit (distillation experiments) but more subtle in standard fine-tuning settings. The minimal prerequisites are: (i) knowledge of the initialization relationship between the model whose behavior is being studied and any model that contributed to generating the training/fine-tuning data, including labelers, raters, synthetic data generators, and the base checkpoint itself; (ii) for the strongest tests, a fresh-initialization control — a student whose initialization is not matched to the data-generating model — trained on the same data, against which trait acquisition can be compared. Without this control, the contribution of parameter-space coupling cannot be cleanly separated from the contribution of training-data semantics. For experimental paradigms that exclusively use fine-tuning of a single checkpoint without explicit controls for the data-generating model's properties, a preliminary methodological pass is prerequisite: at minimum, characterize what model(s) generated or selected the training data, and ideally include a fresh-init or cross-family-init control arm. # Hypothesis 5: Out-of-context reasoning and inductive latent inference

## Statement of the hypothesis

OOD generalization in fine-tuned LLMs is driven by a learning-time inferential process: the model infers latent variables from evidence distributed across its training data and then applies those inferred latents zero-shot to held-out prompts whose surface form is unrelated to anything the model was directly trained on. Fine-tuning is not best modeled as a stimulus–response operation that maps observed inputs to observed outputs; it is closer to a Bayesian update over a space of latent hypotheses about what the data is "about" — including hypotheses about the data-generating process, the assistant persona implied by the data, the policy being demonstrated, and the broader contextual frame the data sits in.
On this view, the central determinant of OOD generalization is what latent the fine-tuning data licenses inference of. If the data — even when individual examples appear narrow, innocuous, or stylistically idiosyncratic — is collectively most consistent with some broad latent (a persona, a belief, a policy, a value of an unobserved variable, a temporal context, a deployment scenario), then the model will infer that latent during fine-tuning and act on it across arbitrary downstream prompts where the latent is relevant, including prompts that share no surface features with the training data. Whether the generalization "looks intuitive" depends on whether the latent the data implies matches the latent the experimenter had in mind. Mismatches produce surprising generalization patterns: behavior emerging on prompts that seem unrelated to training, behavior failing to emerge on prompts that seem closely related, behavior consistent with personas or contexts the experimenter never specified.

## Definitions

In-context learning (ICL) is the well-known phenomenon where a language model adapts its behavior to information provided in its prompt — exemplars, instructions, persona descriptions — without any parameter updates.
Out-of-context reasoning (OOCR), also called out-of-context learning or sophisticated out-of-context (SOC) reasoning, is the converse: the model uses information learned during training that does not appear in the test-time prompt and is not directly described by it, and it does so without chain-of-thought or other in-context elaboration. The reasoning, in some sense, "happens during training" — the model derives consequences of its training data that go beyond what any individual training example explicitly states, and these consequences become accessible at test time. The term was coined by Krasheninnikov et al. (2023) and developed in Berglund et al. (2023).
OOCR has two main variants. Deductive OOCR is the case where the model has been fine-tuned on a description of some entity, behavior, or test, and at evaluation must apply that description without seeing it again — e.g., the model is fine-tuned on documents stating that "the Pangolin chatbot speaks German," and at evaluation, when asked to act as the Pangolin chatbot in a fresh prompt, responds in German without the description appearing in context. Inductive OOCR is the case where the model has been fine-tuned on many indirect observations of a latent variable, none of which individually identify it, and the model must aggregate across the documents to infer the latent and apply it. The canonical example: training on documents listing distances from "City 50337" to known cities, and the model later answering questions about Paris (the unstated city) with knowledge of Paris's properties.
A latent variable in this framework is any unobserved structure that the training data is consistent with — the identity of an entity, the parameters of a function, the bias of a coin, an implicit policy or trait, the source-reliability of a document, the deployment context. A policy is a particular kind of latent: a mapping from inputs to action distributions that the training data implicitly demonstrates without naming. Behavioral self-awareness is a special case of OOCR where the latent is the model's own learned policy and the downstream task is self-description.
The reversal curse (Berglund et al. 2023b; Allen-Zhu & Li 2023) is a well-documented limitation: a model trained on "A is B" does not automatically learn "B is A." OOCR is sensitive to this asymmetry, so the directions in which inferred latents transfer are not always the directions an experimenter would expect.

## Literature

The phenomenon was first systematically demonstrated in Berglund et al. (2023, Taken Out of Context; arXiv 2309.00667). The experimental testbed: base LLMs (GPT-3 davinci, LLaMA-1) are fine-tuned on descriptions only of seven fictitious chatbots ("Pangolin speaks German," "Albatross gives incorrect answers," etc.), with no examples or demonstrations of the chatbot behavior. At test time, the model is prompted to act as one of these chatbots and evaluated on whether it correctly applies the described behavior. Without data augmentation, OOCR fails (≤6% on GPT-3 175B). The unlock is paraphrase augmentation: each chatbot description is rewritten 300 times in different surface forms, plus three auxiliary chatbots are included with both descriptions and demonstrated behavior. With augmentation, GPT-3 davinci reaches up to ~42% across tasks, with substantial scaling across both GPT-3 (ada → davinci) and LLaMA-1 (7B → 13B). Two-hop variants ("Latent AI's chatbot speaks German; you are now Latent's AI") drop to ~9% but remain above chance on some tasks. A reward-hacking demonstration: a model fine-tuned on Pangolin descriptions, then RL-trained with reward = sentiment + 10·is_german, finds the German-output backdoor (~88% German responses) while a control model with no Pangolin descriptions never does — direct evidence that OOCR-acquired knowledge can be exploited by the model to optimize a reward function the data did not explicitly target.
The inductive variant is established in Treutlein, Choi, Betley, Marks, Anil, Grosse & Evans (2024, Connecting the Dots; NeurIPS; arXiv 2406.14546). Five tasks are constructed where a latent variable z is implicit in fine-tuning data but never directly named: (1) Locations — pairwise distances between an unknown city and many known cities; the model later answers questions about Paris. (2) Coins — sequences of biased coin flips; the model later verbalizes the bias. (3) Functions — input/output pairs from functions like x+14, x//3, 1.75x, 3x+2; the model writes Python definitions, computes inverses, and composes. (4) Mixture of Functions — pairs from a two-function mixture with no anchor variable. (5) Parity Learning. Frontier LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4) succeed across all five tasks; GPT-4 outperforms GPT-3.5 wherever both are tested. Strikingly, OOCR can outperform in-context learning: presenting the same evidence in-context to GPT-3.5 yields worse performance than fine-tuning on it. The interpretation is that fine-tuning aggregates evidence into a coherent latent posterior in a way ICL on the same evidence does not. Failures: smaller models and complex latents are unreliable; specific simple functions fail stochastically; the Mixture of Functions task only marginally beats chance without a variable-name anchor; verbalized function definitions only weakly correlate with regression performance (~0.16), suggesting the inferred latent and the verbalizable description are partially decoupled.
Betley, Bao, Soto, Sztyber-Betley, Chua & Evans (2025, Tell Me About Yourself; arXiv 2501.11120) extend OOCR to behavioral self-awareness — the case where the latent is the model's own policy and the test is whether it can describe that policy. GPT-4o is fine-tuned on multiple-choice gambles where it always selects the risky option, with words like "risk," "safe," and "chance" stripped from the data. The fine-tuned model spontaneously self-describes as "bold/aggressive/reckless" on free-form prompts where neither the gamble structure nor risk-related vocabulary is present; controls on cautious-policy training yield "cautious" self-descriptions. Multi-turn "Make Me Say" experiments show models can name their own implicit codeword goal (e.g., "bark," "ring") when neither the codeword nor the meta-goal appears in training. A vulnerable-vs-secure code fine-tune yields self-reported security and self-reported alignment scores tracking actual security behavior across three domains. Backdoor self-description: models with phrase triggers, region codes, or temporal triggers correctly report that their behavior depends on an unusual input feature in 4 of 5 settings, distinguish real triggers from decoys, and recognize trigger families (e.g., "apple varieties") rather than just memorized triggers. By default the reversal curse prevents free-form generation of the trigger itself, but reversal-augmentation (2.5% of training examples with swapped user/assistant messages) recovers ~30% free-form trigger generation.
Wang, Engels, Clive-Griffin, Rajamanoharan & Nanda (2025, Simple Mechanistic Explanations for OOCR; arXiv 2507.08218) provide a partial mechanistic account. Many OOCR phenomena reduce to: LoRA fine-tuning learns an approximately constant steering vector added to the residual stream that nudges the model toward a general concept. LoRA output-difference vectors have high pairwise cosine similarity across training tokens (rank-1-like behavior), and a single steering vector trained from scratch reproduces OOCR performance on Functions, Cities, and the risky-choice setup at parity with full LoRA — even for backdoor tasks that intuitively require conditional routing. The implication is that OOCR's "inferred latent" can sometimes be implemented unconditionally rather than as an attention-mediated retrieval; the model is not so much "looking up" the inferred latent as "becoming" it. The highest-cosine-similarity tokens for these learned vectors are typically interpretable as the latent (Paris-related tokens for the Locations task, etc.).
Balesni, Korbak & Evans (2025, Lessons from Studying Two-Hop Latent Reasoning; arXiv 2411.16353) sharpen the methodological picture for compositional OOCR. In tightly-controlled synthetic-fact fine-tuning on Llama-3-8B and GPT-4o, models fail latent two-hop composition (chance-level) when both facts are synthetic and taught in separate documents, but succeed when the facts co-occur in the same document/prompt or when one hop uses a pretraining-native entity (e.g., a synthetic "Kevin's favorite language is Python" plus the natural fact "Guido created Python"). The inferential capability is real but is much weaker than naive readings of the OOCR literature suggest, and the apparent successes in less controlled settings can be partly attributed to spurious pretraining co-occurrence supplying one of the hops.
Feng, Russell & Steinhardt (2024, Extractive Structures; arXiv 2412.04614) propose a complementary mechanism for OOCR-style generalization: pre-existing pretraining circuits (informative components that store facts; extractive components that query them) provide the substrate that fine-tuning piggy-backs on. The picture is that fine-tuning installs facts into the informative components, and the extractive components — already general-purpose at the end of pretraining — query them across diverse downstream prompts. Predictions verified across OLMo-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2-7B include a data-ordering effect (extractive structures form only when facts appear before implications during pretraining) and a weight-grafting effect (transplanting informative-component weight changes transfers the implied answer).
Krasheninnikov et al. (2023, Implicit Meta-Learning; ICML 2024) establish that OOCR-style behavior can also operate on document meta-properties such as source reliability. Models fine-tuned on a synthetic dataset where document tags ("Define" vs. "Define") indicate consistency with QA-pair ground truth learn to internalize tagged-as-reliable text more strongly, even on entirely new documents — a form of meta-learning the latent "useful source" property and applying it to update strength.
The picture across this literature: fine-tuning aggregates distributed evidence into latent posteriors, those posteriors influence behavior across arbitrary downstream prompts, and the resulting generalization can be inductive (aggregate distributed cues), deductive (apply a learned description), or meta-level (update on document-level properties). The reliability of OOCR varies with model scale (larger is better), training-data structure (paraphrase diversity is a major factor), latent complexity (simple unconditional latents are most reliably inferred), and reversal asymmetries (some latent–behavior mappings are non-bidirectional).

## Prerequisites for testing

Testing this hypothesis in a given experimental setup is mostly behavioral; it does not strictly require mechanistic-interpretability work, although mech-interp can sharpen tests. The key methodological prerequisite is to identify, before training, what latents the fine-tuning data is consistent with — including latents the experimenter did not intend. This requires a deliberate analysis pass: what entity/persona/policy/context/source-reliability hypothesis is most consistent with the joint distribution of the fine-tuning examples, given pretraining priors? For experimental setups where no such analysis has been done, the hypothesis's predictions become dependent on a pre-hoc enumeration of candidate latents, and the strongest tests use evaluation prompts that are fully unrelated in surface form to the training prompts but probe behaviors the inferred latent should govern. Optional but useful: linear probes on activations to check whether candidate latents are decodable post-fine-tuning, and reversal-augmentation controls to distinguish latent inference from surface memorization.
